question: For a 16-QAM modulation with average power normalized to 1, calculate the symbol error rate in an AWGN channel at an SNR of 20 dB. What assumptions are you making?
required_points:
P1: States the SNR assumption: the 20 dB is the per-symbol SNR Es/N0 (average symbol energy 1 over the noise power), so the linear SNR is 100.
P2: States at least two further modelling assumptions, for example a square (4x4) Gray-mapped 16-QAM constellation, equiprobable symbols, AWGN only, or coherent minimum-distance detection with perfect carrier and timing synchronisation.
P3: Uses the square M-QAM symbol error formula, SER = 1 - (1 - p)^2 with p = 2(1 - 1/sqrt(M)) Q(sqrt(3 SNR/(M - 1))) = 1.5 Q(sqrt(20)), or its nearest-neighbour form 3 Q(sqrt(SNR/5)), which gives the same value here to three significant figures.
P4: Evaluates the Q-function argument as sqrt(20), about 4.47, with Q(4.47) about 3.9e-6.
disqualifying_errors: D1: Converts 20 dB to a linear power ratio other than 100 (for example 10, by using 20 log10 for a power ratio).
numeric_tolerance: Symbol error rate 1.16e-5 within 5 % relative (full credit 1.10e-5 to 1.22e-5; two-figure answers such as 1.2e-5 pass). The union bound 4Q(sqrt(20)) = 1.55e-5 and an Eb/N0 reading of the 20 dB (about 5.6e-19) fall outside.
sources:
Proakis and Salehi, Digital Communications, 5th ed., ch. 4: symbol error probability of square M-ary QAM in AWGN, P_M = 1 - (1 - P_sqrtM)^2 with P_sqrtM = 2(1 - 1/sqrt(M)) Q(sqrt(3 Es/((M - 1) N0)))
Goldsmith, Wireless Communications, section 6.1 (M-QAM error probability and its nearest-neighbour approximation)
confirmed value 1.16e-05 (calc_confirmed.jsonl, decided by EX), read after the tolerance was set; the tolerance is the writer's own, not taken from the key
checker_1_source: Proakis and Salehi, Digital Communications, 5th ed., ch. 4 (square M-QAM in AWGN): P_M = 1 - (1 - P_sqrtM)^2, P_sqrtM = 2(1 - 1/sqrt(M)) Q(sqrt(3 Es/((M-1) N0))). With Es/N0 = 20 dB = 100 and M = 16: P_sqrtM = 1.5 Q(sqrt(20)), SER = 1.1616e-5 (my code); confirmed value 1.16e-5 in calc_confirmed.jsonl.
checker_1_note:
note: Recomputed: Q(sqrt(20)) = 3.87e-6, exact SER 1.1616e-5, nearest-neighbour 3Q(sqrt(20)) = 1.1616e-5, union bound 4Q(sqrt(20)) = 1.55e-5, Eb/N0 reading 5.6e-19. All numbers in P3, P4 and the tolerance text are right. numeric gives full credit to the confirmed 1.16e-5; 5 % relative fits two-figure error-rate answers and still excludes the union bound (33 % off) and the Eb/N0 reading. P1 and P2 answer the 'what assumptions' part, as the EX note on the calculation asks. D1 (wrong dB-to-linear conversion) is a real error.

question: Explain differential coding and why it is used in digital modulation. How does it affect the constellation diagram of a PSK signal?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that differential coding carries the information in the change (phase transition) between consecutive symbols, not in the absolute phase of each symbol (for example d_k = d_(k-1) XOR b_k for binary data, or phase_k = phase_(k-1) + delta(b_k) for M-PSK).
P2 (w=2): States that it is used because the receiver's carrier recovery (for example a Costas loop) locks with an unknown phase ambiguity (180 degrees for BPSK, a multiple of 90 degrees for QPSK), and coding the data in phase changes makes the decoded bits independent of that ambiguity; it also allows differential detection without an absolute phase reference.
P3: States that, for standard differential PSK (DBPSK, DQPSK), the constellation diagram shows the same M-PSK points; what changes is the bit-to-point relation: bits select the move from the previous point, not a fixed point, so a rotation of the received constellation by a multiple of 360/M degrees does not change the decoded data.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that differential coding (or differential detection) gives a lower bit error rate than coherent PSK with a known phase reference.
sources:

It makes demodulation easier by avoiding the challenges of absolute phase recovery caused by phase offsets and ambiguities between the transmitter and receiver."
~/grc-agent/docs/wiki_gnuradio_org/PSK_Demodulation.md :: "Therefore, differential encoding simplifies demodulation at the cost of higher bit error rates."

question: Compare the performance of BPSK and QPSK in an AWGN channel at the same bit rate. Which has better BER performance and why?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that, with coherent detection and Gray coding, QPSK has the same bit error rate as BPSK at the same Eb/N0: Pb = Q(sqrt(2 Eb/N0)) for both.
P2: Explains why: QPSK is two BPSK signals on orthogonal (I and Q) carriers, each carrying one bit with energy Eb, so the noise on one axis does not affect the bit on the other and each bit sees the same distance-to-noise ratio as in BPSK.
P3: States that at the same bit rate QPSK sends half as many symbols per second, so it needs about half the bandwidth (twice the spectral efficiency) of BPSK for the same BER.
P4: States that BPSK looks 3 dB better only when the two are compared at the same per-symbol SNR (Es/N0), because a QPSK symbol carries two bits (Es = 2 Eb).
disqualifying_errors: D1: Concludes that BPSK has a better bit error rate than Gray-coded QPSK at the same Eb/N0 (same bit rate and transmit power).
sources:
Proakis and Salehi, Digital Communications, 5th ed., ch. 4: bit error probability of BPSK and of Gray-coded QPSK, both Q(sqrt(2 Eb/N0))
Sklar, Digital Communications, 2nd ed., ch. 4 (BPSK and QPSK bit error performance)
PySDR (Lichtman), chapter 'Digital Modulation' (QPSK as two BPSK signals in I and Q)
checker_1_source: Proakis and Salehi, Digital Communications, 5th ed., ch. 4: BPSK Pb = Q(sqrt(2Eb/N0)); Gray-coded QPSK is two orthogonal BPSK channels with the same Pb. Checked with my own Monte Carlo below.
checker_1_note: note: P1 (equal BER at equal Eb/N0), P2 (I and Q are independent BPSK channels), P3 (half the symbol rate, half the bandwidth) and P4 (the 3 dB difference appears only at equal Es/N0) are all right and each decidable. 'Same bit rate' with the same power fixes Eb, so the question is answerable. D1 is the confusion the question tests.
checker_2_source: Proakis and Salehi, Digital Communications 5th ed., ch. 4: Pb(BPSK) = Q(sqrt(2Eb/N0)) and Gray-coded QPSK has the same bit error probability; derivation: QPSK = two orthogonal BPSK streams, each bit with energy Eb, so Pb = Q(sqrt(2Eb/N0)) for both; at the same bit rate QPSK has half the symbol rate, so half the bandwidth.
checker_2_note: note: All four points are right and each is one checkable idea. D1 is the confusion the question tests. P4 (3 dB difference only at equal Es/N0) is right since Es = 2Eb for QPSK. Chapter citations are at chapter level and correct (Proakis ch. 4; Sklar ch. 4 covers bandpass detection and binary/M-ary error performance; PySDR has a 'Digital Modulation' chapter).

question: What is the purpose of the 10 MHz and PPS synchronization inputs on USRP devices? How do they improve the performance of distributed SDR systems?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that the 10 MHz input is a frequency reference: the USRP locks its reference clock, and so its LO synthesizers and sample clock, to the external 10 MHz signal, so that several devices share one frequency standard and have no relative frequency offset or drift.
P2 (w=2): States that the PPS (pulse-per-second) input is a time reference: its edge sets or aligns the device's time counter, so that sample timestamps and timed commands (for example a timed stream start) are aligned across devices.
P3: Explains the benefit for distributed or multi-device systems: with a common frequency and aligned time, the channels of several USRPs can be combined coherently (MIMO, phased arrays and beamforming, TDOA localisation), which free-running clocks would prevent.
P4: States that a GPS-disciplined oscillator (GPSDO), on board or external, can supply both the 10 MHz and the PPS, which allows synchronisation of nodes that are far apart.
disqualifying_errors: D1: Swaps the roles of the two inputs (says the PPS sets the frequency or clock rate, or that the 10 MHz aligns time).

question: Why do we use a logarithmic scale (dB) for representing power and amplitude in wireless communications? Provide at least three practical reasons.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Gives at least three distinct, valid practical reasons for using dB (for example those in P2 and P3, the logarithmic decay of path loss with distance, the logarithmic perception of loudness, or the convenience of showing weak and strong signals on one spectrum plot).
P2: States that powers in radio systems span many orders of magnitude (for example watts at the transmitter, picowatts or less at the receiver), and the logarithmic scale compresses this dynamic range into small, readable numbers.
P3: States that gains and losses that multiply in linear units add and subtract in dB, which makes cascades and link budgets simple sums.

question: Explain variance and standard deviation. How are they related, and what do they tell us about a random variable?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that the variance is the expected (mean) squared deviation from the mean, sigma^2 = E[(X - mu)^2] = E[X^2] - mu^2 (for samples, the mean of the squared deviations, with N - 1 in the denominator for the unbiased estimate).
P2 (w=2): States that the standard deviation is the square root of the variance, sigma = sqrt(sigma^2), and so has the same units as the variable, while the variance has squared units.
P3: States that both measure how widely the values spread around the mean (a small value means the values cluster near the mean).
disqualifying_errors: D1: Inverts the relation (says the variance is the square root of the standard deviation, or the standard deviation is the square of the variance).
sources:
Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing, ch. 2 'Statistics, Probability and Noise' (mean, standard deviation, variance; variance as the power of the fluctuation)
PySDR (Lichtman), chapter 'Noise and Random Variables' (variance of zero-mean noise equals its power)
checker_1_source: Papoulis and Pillai, Probability, Random Variables and Stochastic Processes, 4th ed., ch. 5 (variance sigma^2 = E[(X - mu)^2], standard deviation sigma); Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to DSP, ch. 2.

P4: delete -- the question asks about a random variable in general; the link to signal power and RMS is true but not asked, and an answer that fully covers definition, relation and meaning would lose a sixth of the score.
note: P1 (variance as the mean squared deviation), P2 (standard deviation is its square root, same units as the variable) and P3 (spread around the mean, 68 % within one sigma for a Gaussian) are right and answer the three parts. P4 is true for zero-mean signals but is not asked. D1 (inverted relation) is a real error.

question: For a complex random variable Z = X + jY where X and Y are independent Gaussian random variables with mean 0 and variance σ², what is the distribution of Z? What are its statistical properties?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that Z is a circularly symmetric complex Gaussian random variable, Z ~ CN(0, 2 sigma^2).
P2 (w=2): Gives its mean and variance: E[Z] = 0 and E[|Z|^2] = E[X^2] + E[Y^2] = 2 sigma^2.
P3: States the circular-symmetry property: the pseudo-variance E[Z^2] = E[X^2] - E[Y^2] + 2j E[XY] = 0, so the distribution of e^(j theta) Z is the same as that of Z for any rotation theta.
P4: Gives the density f(z) = 1/(2 pi sigma^2) exp(-|z|^2/(2 sigma^2)), the product of the densities of X and Y.
P5: States that the magnitude |Z| is Rayleigh distributed (parameter sigma, mean sigma sqrt(pi/2)), the phase is uniform on [0, 2 pi) and independent of the magnitude, and |Z|^2 is exponential with mean 2 sigma^2.

question: How does channel coding affect the overall latency of a communication system? What are the tradeoffs between latency and error correction capability?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that channel coding adds latency mainly because the decoder must collect a whole codeword or block (or an interleaver span, or a Viterbi traceback depth) before it can output decoded bits, so delay grows with block length, interleaver depth or constraint length, plus the decoding computation time (more for iterative decoders such as turbo and LDPC).
P2: States that the redundancy lowers the information rate for a fixed symbol rate (code rate k/n < 1), so the same payload takes longer to send or needs more bandwidth.
P3 (w=2): States the trade-off: stronger codes (longer blocks, lower rates, longer constraint lengths, deeper interleaving against burst errors) correct more errors and come closer to capacity, but cost more delay; short blocks give low latency but weaker correction.
P4: States the choice by application: delay-sensitive services (voice, control, low-latency links) use short codes or limited interleaving, delay-tolerant ones (file transfer, broadcast, deep space) long codes; forward error correction also avoids the round-trip delay of retransmissions (ARQ), and HARQ combines both.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that longer codewords, deeper interleaving or a longer constraint length reduce the encoding and decoding delay.

Polyanskiy, Poor and Verdu, 'Channel coding rate in the finite blocklength regime', IEEE Trans. Information Theory 56(5), 2010 (achievable rate falls as block length shrinks)
PySDR (Lichtman), chapter 'Channel Coding' (code rate and the cost of redundancy)

question: What is a root raised-cosine filter, and how does it differ from a standard raised-cosine filter? What are the advantages of using RRC filters in a communication system?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that a root raised-cosine (RRC) filter has a frequency response equal to the square root of the raised-cosine (RC) response, so two RRC filters in cascade (transmitter and receiver) give an overall raised-cosine response.
P2: States that the raised-cosine pulse meets the Nyquist zero-ISI criterion (its impulse response is zero at all nonzero multiples of the symbol period), while a single RRC filter does not; only the RRC-RRC cascade is free of ISI.
P3 (w=2): States the main advantage: with RRC at both ends the receive filter is matched to the transmit pulse, which maximises SNR at the sampling instant, while the cascade still has zero ISI.
P4: States that the roll-off (excess bandwidth) factor alpha, between 0 and 1, sets the occupied bandwidth (1 + alpha) times the symbol rate (passband; half that at baseband), trading bandwidth against the length of the pulse tails and sensitivity to timing error.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that a single RRC filter is free of ISI on its own, or recommends a full raised-cosine filter at both the transmitter and the receiver.

Proakis and Salehi, Digital Communications, 5th ed., ch. 9 (Nyquist criterion, raised-cosine spectrum, split between transmitter and receiver filters)

question: What is an eye diagram, and how is it used to evaluate the performance of a digital communication system? What information can you extract from an eye diagram?

P1 (w=2): States that an eye diagram overlays many short segments (typically one or two symbol periods long) of the received, filtered baseband waveform, triggered by the symbol clock, so that all the symbol transitions are drawn on top of each other.

question: Explain the principle of fine frequency synchronization. What are the key algorithms and techniques used, and what are their tradeoffs?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that fine frequency synchronisation removes the small residual carrier frequency offset (and the phase offset) left after coarse correction, so that the constellation stops rotating, usually with a closed loop that tracks phase and frequency.
P2 (w=2): Describes the key algorithm, the Costas loop (or a decision-directed PLL): a phase error detector (for BPSK the product of the real and imaginary parts of the output, for QPSK a sign-based or decision-based error), a second-order loop filter (proportional and integral gains, alpha and beta), and an NCO/phase accumulator that rotates the samples by exp(-j phase).
P3: Names other techniques: data-aided estimation on pilots or preambles, and feedforward (open-loop) estimators that estimate the offset from a block of samples.
P4 (w=2): States the trade-offs: a wide loop bandwidth acquires faster and pulls in larger offsets but lets more noise through (more phase jitter), a narrow loop is cleaner but slower; decision-directed loops degrade at low SNR and leave an M-fold phase ambiguity (resolved by differential coding or pilots); feedback loops track drift, feedforward estimators acquire quickly but need a block of data.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that a wider loop bandwidth gives lower phase jitter (less noise), or that a narrower loop acquires faster.

question: What are the tradeoffs between using a 2D planar array versus multiple 1D arrays for beamforming? Consider factors such as complexity, cost, and performance.

question: What is cyclostationary processing, and what makes a signal cyclostationary? Provide examples of signals that exhibit cyclostationarity.

P2: States what causes the periodicity: the structure of man-made signals, such as the symbol rate of a pulse train, the carrier frequency, a spreading chip rate, OFDM symbol timing from the cyclic prefix, frames or pilots.
P3 (w=2): Gives at least two correct examples of cyclostationary signals, such as BPSK (features at the symbol rate, conjugate features at twice the carrier), QPSK/QAM (symbol rate), AM (twice the carrier), OFDM with a cyclic prefix, DSSS (chip rate) or radar pulse trains.
P4: Names the main tools and uses: the cyclic autocorrelation function and the spectral correlation function (estimated for example by frequency smoothing, the FFT accumulation method or SSCA), used for detection at low SNR, signal classification and estimating parameters such as the symbol rate.

question: Explain the concept of cyclic autocorrelation. How is it different from regular autocorrelation, and what information does it provide?

P1 (w=2): Defines the cyclic autocorrelation function: R_x^alpha(tau) = lim (1/T) integral of x(t + tau/2) x*(t - tau/2) exp(-j 2 pi alpha t) dt (or a discrete-time average of x[n + tau] x*[n] exp(-j 2 pi alpha n)), the Fourier-series coefficient at cycle frequency alpha of the time-varying autocorrelation.
P2 (w=2): States the difference: the ordinary autocorrelation is the alpha = 0 case (a time average) and hides any periodic variation of the statistics; at alpha other than 0 the CAF measures the correlation between spectral components separated by alpha, and it is nonzero only for cyclostationary signals.
P3: States the information it gives: the cycle frequencies with nonzero CAF reveal hidden periodicities (symbol rate, carrier, chip rate), which allows detection at low SNR (stationary noise and interference give no feature), classification and parameter estimation.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that stationary noise produces cyclic autocorrelation peaks at nonzero cycle frequencies.

P4: States how it is used for direction finding: for closely spaced sensors and a far-field source, the time difference gives the angle of arrival, delta_t = d sin(theta) / c (for a narrowband signal, a phase difference).

question: Explain how superposition enables frequency-domain analysis for linear systems and why it's not applicable to nonlinear systems.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States the superposition principle of linear systems: additivity and homogeneity, T{a x1 + b x2} = a T{x1} + b T{x2}.
P2 (w=2): Explains how it enables frequency-domain analysis: the input is decomposed into sinusoids (complex exponentials, the eigenfunctions of LTI systems), each passes through the system changed only in amplitude and phase by H(f) at its own frequency, and by superposition the output is the sum of these responses, Y(f) = H(f) X(f) (convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency).
P3 (w=2): Explains why it fails for nonlinear systems: the response to a sum is not the sum of the responses, and a sinusoid comes out with new frequency components (harmonics and intermodulation products, for example squaring two tones f1 and f2 gives 2f1, 2f2, f1 + f2, f1 - f2 and DC), so no single frequency response H(f) describes the system.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that a nonlinear system can be described by a transfer function H(f), or that it produces no new frequency components.

question: A real-valued signal has a DFT with Hermitian symmetry. Explain what this means and how it can be exploited to reduce computation and storage.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States the Hermitian symmetry of the DFT of a real signal: X[N - k] = X*[k] (X[-k] = X*[k]), so the real part is even, the imaginary part odd, the magnitude even and the phase odd, and X[0] (and X[N/2] for even N) is real.
P2 (w=2): States the storage saving: only bins 0 to N/2 (N/2 + 1 complex values) are independent, so only half the spectrum needs to be stored (as numpy.fft.rfft does); the other half follows by conjugation.
P3 (w=2): States the computation saving of about half: an N-point real FFT can be computed with an N/2-point complex FFT (even and odd samples packed as real and imaginary parts) plus a post-processing step, or two real signals can be transformed with one complex FFT of x1 + j x2 and separated using the symmetry.
P4: States that the inverse also benefits: to synthesise a real signal only the non-negative-frequency half of the spectrum must be specified (for example numpy.fft.irfft).
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that the DFT of a real-valued signal is itself real-valued.

question: Explain how the DFT can be used to implement a filter in the frequency domain, and when this approach might be preferable to time-domain filtering.

P1 (w=2): States the method: take the DFT of the signal, multiply it by the filter's frequency response (the DFT of its impulse response), and take the inverse DFT (the convolution theorem).
P2 (w=2): States that multiplying DFTs gives circular convolution, so for linear convolution both sequences must be zero-padded to at least L + M - 1 points (signal length L, filter length M), and long or streaming signals are processed in blocks with overlap-add or overlap-save.

question: Explain the concept of the sinc function and its importance in signal processing, particularly in filter design.
required_points:
P1: Defines the sinc function: sinc(x) = sin(pi x)/(pi x) (normalised form; sin(x)/x unnormalised), equal to 1 at x = 0, zero at the other integers, with oscillations decaying as 1/x.
P2 (w=2): States the Fourier pair: a rectangular pulse has a sinc spectrum, and the ideal low-pass filter (rectangular frequency response) has a sinc impulse response, h[n] = 2 fc sinc(2 fc n) with fc the cutoff as a fraction of the sample rate.
P3 (w=2): States its role in filter design: the ideal sinc is infinitely long and non-causal, so FIR design truncates it, multiplies it by a window (for example Blackman or Hamming) and shifts it to be causal (the windowed-sinc method); plain truncation causes passband ripple and stopband sidelobes (the Gibbs effect).
P4: Names another role: ideal (Whittaker-Shannon) reconstruction of a sampled signal is sinc interpolation, and a zero-order hold (DAC) has a sinc-shaped frequency response that droops and may need compensation.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that the ideal low-pass filter's impulse response is finite or causal, so it can be implemented exactly without truncation.

Oppenheim and Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed., section 7.5 (FIR design by windowing the ideal impulse response)

question: Explain the Gibbs effect in the context of Fourier series and DFT, and how it manifests in practical signal processing.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States the Gibbs effect: when a signal with a discontinuity (for example a square wave) is built from a finite number of Fourier components, the partial sum overshoots and rings next to the discontinuity, and the overshoot stays at about 9 % of the jump however many terms are added; the ripples only become narrower.
P2: Explains the cause: truncating the spectrum is multiplying it by a rectangular window, which convolves the signal with a sinc, and the sinc's oscillating sidelobes produce the ripple.
P3 (w=2): Describes how it shows up in practice: when a signal is rebuilt from a limited set of DFT bins (or band-limited by zeroing bins), and, by duality, in FIR design where truncating the ideal sinc impulse response gives passband and stopband ripple near the cutoff that does not shrink with more taps; also ringing in the step response of sharp filters and ringing artefacts in audio and images.
P4: Names the remedy and its cost: a smooth window or taper (Hamming, Blackman, Kaiser) reduces the ripple at the price of a wider transition band.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that the overshoot goes to zero as more Fourier terms (or filter taps) are used.

question: Design a recursive implementation of a moving average filter and compare its computational efficiency to the non-recursive version.

question: Explain how the choice of window function affects the Gibbs effect in windowed-sinc filters, and how this relates to the filter's frequency response.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that truncating the sinc abruptly (a rectangular window) causes the Gibbs effect: ripple and overshoot near the cutoff in the passband and stopband sidelobes of only about -21 dB, which do not shrink as taps are added.
P2 (w=2): States that smooth tapered windows (Hann, Hamming, Blackman, Kaiser) reduce the ripple and sidelobes (about -53 dB for Hamming, about -74 dB for Blackman), because the windowed filter's response is the ideal response convolved with the window's spectrum, whose sidelobes set the ripple and attenuation.
P3 (w=2): States the trade-off: lower sidelobes come with a wider main lobe of the window spectrum, so the transition band widens for the same number of taps (Blackman wider than Hamming); the number of taps sets the transition width, and the Kaiser window's beta parameter trades the two continuously.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that adding taps to a rectangular-windowed sinc removes the Gibbs overshoot or ripple.
numeric_tolerance: The window figures are approximate: rectangular about -21 dB, Hamming about -53 dB, Blackman about -74 dB peak stopband error; values within about 3 dB of these are correct.

question: Explain how the concept of least squares can be applied to filter design, and what advantages this approach offers over other methods.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that least-squares design chooses the filter coefficients that minimise the (weighted) integrated squared error between the desired and the actual frequency response, E = integral of W(omega) |H(e^(j omega)) - D(omega)|^2 d omega (or a sum over a dense frequency grid), with transition bands left as 'don't care'.
P2: States that for a linear-phase FIR filter the error is quadratic in the coefficients, so the optimum is found by solving a linear system (the normal equations) in closed form, without iteration (for example scipy.signal.firls).
P3 (w=2): States the advantages: the least total error energy, a simple and reliable computation, and easy handling of arbitrary desired responses and per-band weights; compared with equiripple (Parks-McClellan, minimax) design it gives a lower integrated squared error but a larger peak error near the band edges.

question: Explain how a narrow-band recursive filter can be designed, and what applications such filters are particularly suited for.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Describes the design by pole-zero placement: a band-pass (resonator) uses a complex-conjugate pole pair at radius r close to 1 and angle +/- 2 pi f0/fs; a notch (band-reject) puts zeros on the unit circle at that angle with poles just inside it; for example Smith's narrow-band filter with R = 1 - 3 BW and coefficients from R and cos(2 pi f).
P2 (w=2): States that the pole radius sets the bandwidth: the closer r is to 1, the narrower the band (the -3 dB bandwidth is about 2(1 - r) rad/sample, that is (1 - r) fs / pi).
P3: States the advantage: a very narrow band from a second-order section with about five coefficients, where an FIR filter would need hundreds of taps.
P4 (w=2): Names applications suited to it: removing a single interfering frequency (for example a 50/60 Hz mains-hum notch or a tone), or isolating one frequency (a pilot or tone detection such as DTMF, resonators).

question: Explain the key differences in the design approach between FIR and IIR filters, and how these differences affect their use in practical applications.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Describes the FIR design approach: no feedback, a finite impulse response designed directly in discrete time (windowed sinc, frequency sampling, least squares, Parks-McClellan equiripple); it is always stable and can have exactly linear phase with symmetric taps.
P2 (w=2): Describes the IIR design approach: recursive (feedback), usually designed by transforming a classical analog prototype (Butterworth, Chebyshev, elliptic) with the bilinear transform (with prewarping) or impulse invariance, or by pole-zero placement; the phase is nonlinear and the poles must lie inside the unit circle for stability.
P3 (w=2): States the practical consequences: an IIR filter meets a sharp specification with far fewer coefficients (less computation, memory and delay) but brings phase distortion, sensitivity to coefficient quantisation and limit cycles, and possible instability; an FIR filter needs many more taps and more latency but gives linear phase, guaranteed stability and easy fixed-point use.
P4: Gives examples of the resulting choice: FIR where phase matters (pulse shaping and matched filters in data communications, linear-phase audio), IIR where cost and latency matter (simple tone controls and equalisers, DC blockers, control loops).
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that FIR filters can be unstable, or that IIR filters have exactly linear phase.

Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing, ch. 21 'Filter Comparison' (FIR versus IIR: speed, phase, stability)
Oppenheim and Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed., ch. 7 'Filter Design Techniques' (IIR from analog prototypes, FIR by windowing and optimal approximation)

question: Design a digital audio effects processor that modifies the timbre of a signal by enhancing certain frequency components while attenuating others.
required_points:

question: Design a companding system for digital audio that reduces the dynamic range while maintaining perceived sound quality.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States the companding principle: compress the amplitude with a nonlinear (logarithmic) characteristic before quantisation or transmission and expand with the exact inverse after decoding, so small amplitudes get fine quantisation steps and large ones coarse steps.
P2 (w=2): Specifies the compression characteristic, for example mu-law y = sgn(x) ln(1 + mu|x|)/ln(1 + mu) with mu = 255 or A-law with A = 87.6 (ITU-T G.711), as segmented 8-bit codes or lookup tables; or a block (near-instantaneous) companding scheme with scale factors; or a syllabic compander with a level detector, attack and release times and a fixed ratio in dB (for example 2:1) mirrored by the expander.
P3 (w=2): States the result: the SNR stays roughly constant over a wide range of signal levels, so fewer bits (for example 8-bit companded against about 12- to 13-bit linear PCM) give the same perceived quality.
P4: Justifies it perceptually: loudness is perceived roughly logarithmically and the noise relative to the signal level matters, so quantisation noise that scales with the signal is masked by it.
P5: Describes how the design is checked: SNR (or listening tests) versus input level, compared with linear quantisation at the same bit count.
numeric_tolerance: mu = 255 and A = 87.6 are exact; 'about 12 to 13 bits' of linear-equivalent quality is approximate.
sources:

ITU-T Recommendation G.711 (1988), Pulse code modulation (PCM) of voice frequencies (mu-law, A-law)

question: Explain how DSP techniques are used in speech synthesis and recognition, and what challenges are involved in these applications.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Describes the source-filter model of speech: an excitation (periodic glottal pulses at the pitch frequency for voiced sounds, noise for unvoiced sounds) passed through a time-varying vocal-tract filter whose resonances are the formants, analysed in short frames (about 10-30 ms) over which speech is nearly stationary.
P2 (w=2): Describes DSP in synthesis: generating the excitation and filtering it with an all-pole filter whose coefficients come from linear predictive coding (LPC) frame by frame (as in LPC vocoders), or concatenative or formant synthesis.
P3 (w=2): Describes DSP in recognition: a front end that computes features per frame from the short-time spectrum (for example MFCCs or LPC cepstra), followed by pattern matching or classification (dynamic time warping, hidden Markov models, neural networks).
P4: Names the challenges: variation between speakers, accents and speaking rate, coarticulation and word boundaries in continuous speech, background noise and reverberation, natural prosody in synthesis, and real-time computation.

Rabiner and Schafer, Theory and Applications of Digital Speech Processing (Pearson, 2010) (LPC, cepstral features)
Rabiner and Juang, Fundamentals of Speech Recognition (Prentice Hall, 1993)

question: Design a nonlinear audio effects processor that introduces harmonic distortion in a controlled manner to emulate analog equipment.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Uses a nonlinear transfer curve (waveshaper) y = f(x) applied sample by sample, for example soft clipping with tanh(g x), arctan or a cubic, and states that a symmetric (odd) curve produces only odd harmonics while an asymmetric curve (an added bias or even-order term) also produces even harmonics.
P2: Describes the controls: input gain (drive) sets the amount of distortion, with output level compensation and a dry/wet mix (Chebyshev-polynomial waveshaping, which sets each harmonic's level for a full-scale sine, is one example of a curve with exact harmonic control).
P3 (w=2): States that the nonlinearity creates harmonics above the Nyquist frequency that alias back as inharmonic components, and that this is controlled by oversampling (for example 4-8x) with low-pass filtering before downsampling (or band-limited methods).
P4: Describes how analog equipment is emulated beyond the static curve: filtering before and after the nonlinearity (pre-emphasis, tone stack, speaker or cabinet response), level-dependent or memory behaviour, and a DC blocker after asymmetric shaping.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that a symmetric (odd) transfer curve produces even harmonics, or that an asymmetric curve produces only odd harmonics.

question: Explain the structure of digital images and how this affects the types of DSP techniques that can be applied to them.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that a digital image is a two-dimensional array of pixels sampled on a (usually rectangular) grid, each pixel a quantised value (for example 8-bit grey levels 0-255, or three channels such as RGB for colour); the sampling grid sets the spatial resolution.
P2 (w=2): States that, as 2D signals, images are processed with 2D versions of 1D techniques: 2D convolution with small kernels (point spread functions), the 2D Fourier transform computed row by row and column by column, and separable filters applied to rows then columns for efficiency.
P3 (w=2): States how images differ from 1D signals such as audio and what that implies: the information is in the spatial domain (edges, shapes, textures) rather than in frequencies, all pixels are available so non-causal (centred) kernels are natural, images have borders that must be handled, the data volume is large, brightness is non-negative, and point operations on grey levels (brightness, contrast, histogram equalisation) are common.
P4: States that spatial sampling and quantisation limit what processing can recover: undersampling causes aliasing (moire), and coarse grey-level quantisation causes contouring.
sources:
Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing, ch. 23 'Image Formation & Display' (digital image structure, pixels, 8-bit grey levels, brightness and contrast) and ch. 24 'Linear Image Processing' (2D convolution, separability, point spread function)
Gonzalez and Woods, Digital Image Processing, 4th ed. (Pearson, 2018), ch. 2 (image sampling and quantisation) and ch. 3 (intensity transformations, spatial filtering)

question: Explain how different image acquisition methods (e.g., cameras, scanners, medical imaging) affect the DSP techniques used to process the resulting images.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Cameras (CCD/CMOS): states that the sensor samples light directly on a pixel grid, with optical blur, sensor noise and (for colour) a Bayer filter mosaic, so the processing includes demosaicing, denoising, deblurring or sharpening, white balance and lens-distortion correction.
P2: Scanners: states that a scanner acquires line by line at high resolution under controlled lighting, so typical processing is flat-field (illumination) correction, sharpening and removal of moire from halftone prints (descreening by low-pass filtering).
P3 (w=2): Medical imaging: states that many modalities measure indirect data from which the image must be reconstructed, for example computed tomography from projections (filtered back-projection, Fourier slice theorem), MRI from spatial-frequency (k-space) samples by an inverse 2D FFT, ultrasound by beamforming echo times; so the image formation itself is DSP.
P4: States that each modality has its own noise and resolution character (for example Gaussian sensor noise, Poisson counting noise in X-ray/PET, speckle in ultrasound), which decides the filters used (for example median or speckle-reduction filters versus linear smoothing).

question: Explain how linear image processing techniques can be combined to create more sophisticated image enhancement algorithms.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States why linear techniques combine: a cascade of convolutions equals one convolution with the combined kernel (associativity), and a sum of filtered images equals filtering with the summed kernel (distributivity), so complex enhancement can be built from simple kernels.
P2 (w=2): Gives a correct combined algorithm, for example unsharp masking or high-boost filtering: sharpened = original + k (original - blurred), the same as one kernel (1 + k) delta - k (blur kernel); or adding a Laplacian (high-pass) image to the original to enhance edges.
P3: Gives other combinations, for example smoothing before edge detection (Laplacian of Gaussian, difference of Gaussians as a band-pass), separable kernels applied by rows and columns, FFT convolution for large kernels, or linear filtering followed by a contrast (point) operation.

question: Explain how neural networks can be used for target detection in signal processing applications, and what advantages they offer over traditional methods.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Describes how a neural network detects targets: it is trained on labelled examples (target present or absent) to map input samples or features through layers of weighted sums and nonlinear activations to an output score, with the weights found by backpropagation (gradient descent on an error measure), and a threshold on the score gives the detection decision.
P2: States what can be fed to it: raw samples, spectrograms or images, or extracted features; convolutional networks learn their own filters from spectrograms or images.
P3 (w=2): States the advantages: it learns complex nonlinear decision boundaries without an explicit model of the signal and noise, combines many features, and copes with non-Gaussian noise or clutter where model-based detectors are hard to derive.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that a neural network beats the matched filter for a known signal in white Gaussian noise.

question: Explain how LZW compression works and compare it to Huffman encoding in terms of efficiency and implementation complexity.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Describes LZW: a dictionary coder whose table starts with all single symbols (for example 256 byte values); the encoder finds the longest string already in the table, outputs its code and adds that string plus the next symbol as a new entry; the decoder rebuilds the same table from the codes, so the table is never transmitted.
P2 (w=2): Describes Huffman coding: a statistical (entropy) coder that builds a prefix-free variable-length code from the symbol probabilities by repeatedly merging the two least probable symbols, giving short codes to frequent symbols, with an average length within 1 bit per symbol of the entropy; the code table (or the statistics) must be known to the decoder.
P3 (w=2): Compares efficiency: Huffman exploits only unequal symbol frequencies (at least 1 bit per symbol, no context), while LZW exploits repeated strings and adapts in one pass, so LZW wins on data with repeated patterns (text, graphics) and Huffman can win on memoryless data with skewed symbol probabilities; neither compresses noise-like data well.
P4: Compares implementation complexity: Huffman needs the statistics first (two passes or a fixed table), tree construction and bit-level variable-length codes; LZW is single-pass with table lookups (hashing) but needs dictionary memory and a policy when the table fills. (Naming where each is used, for example LZW in GIF and Unix compress, Huffman in JPEG and DEFLATE, is optional.)

question: Design a lossy compression system for audio signals that maintains perceived quality while achieving significant compression ratios.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Uses a time-frequency analysis stage: a filter bank or an MDCT on overlapping windowed blocks, so that the signal is represented as frequency coefficients per block.
P2 (w=2): Uses a psychoacoustic model to find what is inaudible: the absolute threshold of hearing, simultaneous (frequency) masking across critical bands (Bark scale) and temporal masking, giving a masking threshold per band.
P3 (w=2): Allocates bits so that the quantisation noise in each band stays below the masking threshold (noise-to-mask ratio), quantises coarsely where the noise is masked, and entropy-codes (for example Huffman) the quantised values with side information, which gives large ratios (for example CD audio at 1411 kbit/s coded at 128 kbit/s, about 11:1).
P4: Covers the decoder and the design issues: inverse quantisation and inverse transform with overlap-add (MDCT time-domain aliasing cancellation); pre-echo on transients handled by window switching; stereo redundancy (mid/side coding); rate control; and evaluation by listening tests.

question: Explain how the Laplace transform can be used to solve differential equations describing continuous-time systems, and provide an example.

P2 (w=0.5): States that with zero initial conditions this gives the transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s), whose poles give the natural response and stability (poles in the left half-plane) and whose values on s = j omega give the frequency response.

question: Design a digital filter with specified frequency response using z-transform techniques, and explain how the pole-zero placement affects the filter's characteristics.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Describes the method: write H(z) = K prod(1 - z_k z^-1) / prod(1 - p_k z^-1), place the zeros and poles in the z-plane to shape the response, and evaluate H on the unit circle (z = e^(j omega)) to get the frequency response.
P2 (w=2): States how placement shapes the response: a zero on or near the unit circle at angle omega0 makes a null or dip at omega0, a pole near the unit circle at omega0 makes a peak, and the closer they are to the circle the sharper the effect; poles must lie inside the unit circle for a causal stable filter.
P3: States how the filter is obtained from the placement: complex poles and zeros in conjugate pairs for real coefficients, multiplying out to the difference equation y[n] = sum b_k x[n - k] - sum a_k y[n - k], with K chosen for the wanted passband gain (for example unity at DC).
P4: Gives a correct example, for example a notch at omega0 with zeros at e^(+/- j omega0) and poles at r e^(+/- j omega0) with r slightly below 1, or a low-pass with zeros at z = -1 and poles near z = 1.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that a zero produces a peak or a pole produces a null in the magnitude response, or that poles outside the unit circle give a stable causal filter.

question: What is the role of Automatic Frequency Control (AFC) in a direct conversion receiver?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that AFC is a feedback loop that measures the frequency error between the received carrier and the local oscillator and corrects it, by retuning the LO (synthesiser, VCO or VCTCXO) or by a digital frequency shift (NCO) on the I/Q samples, so the downconverted signal stays centred at 0 Hz.
P2 (w=2): Explains why a direct-conversion (zero-IF) receiver needs it: the LO sits at the carrier frequency, so any LO-carrier offset (oscillator tolerance in ppm, temperature drift, Doppler; for example 10 ppm at 900 MHz is 9 kHz) leaves a residual frequency offset at baseband that shifts the signal against the channel filter and makes the constellation rotate; AFC brings the offset within the pull-in range of the demodulator's fine carrier recovery.
P3: States how the error is measured: a frequency discriminator or estimator on the baseband I/Q (for example the phase change between samples or an FFT peak), filtered by a loop filter before the correction.
disqualifying_errors: D1: Describes AFC as controlling signal amplitude or gain (confuses it with automatic gain control).

Razavi, RF Microelectronics, 2nd ed. (Prentice Hall, 2011), ch. 4 (direct-conversion receivers)

question: How does phase noise affect the constellation diagram of a QAM-modulated signal?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that phase noise is a random fluctuation of the oscillator phase that multiplies the signal by e^(j phi(t)), rotating each received symbol by a random angle about the origin.

P3: States the consequence: higher-order QAM (64-QAM, 256-QAM) with closely spaced outer points is more sensitive, giving higher EVM and symbol or bit errors; slow phase drift (inside the carrier loop bandwidth) can be tracked out as a common rotation, while faster phase noise remains (and in OFDM causes a common phase error plus inter-carrier interference).

question: What are the key differences between hard real-time and soft real-time DSP systems?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Defines hard real-time: every deadline must be met, and a single missed deadline is a system failure (for example a control loop, a protocol turnaround or slot timing, a safety system).
P2 (w=2): Defines soft real-time: deadlines should usually be met, and an occasional miss only degrades quality (for example audio or video streaming with buffering, a spectrum display that drops a frame).
P3: States the design consequences: hard real-time needs bounded, deterministic worst-case execution time and latency (an RTOS, bare-metal DSP or FPGA, no unbounded operations such as dynamic allocation or paging), while soft real-time can run on a general-purpose OS with buffering, average-case performance and graceful degradation (dropped samples or frames).

question: How does the use of oversampling in an ADC improve the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of an SDR system?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Explains the mechanism: the quantisation noise power (q^2/12) is spread roughly uniformly (white) from 0 to fs/2, so sampling faster than needed spreads the same noise over a wider band; after a digital low-pass filter to the signal bandwidth B (and decimation) only the fraction 2B/fs = 1/OSR of it remains.
P2 (w=2): Gives the size of the gain: an SNR improvement of 10 log10(OSR) dB, that is about 3 dB per doubling of the sample rate, half a bit of resolution per doubling (one extra bit per factor 4); for a full-scale sine SNR = 6.02 N + 1.76 + 10 log10(fs/(2B)) dB.
P3: States the conditions and limits: the noise must be white and uncorrelated with the signal (enough noise or dither), the digital filter must remove the out-of-band noise, and noise shaping (sigma-delta converters) gives much more than 3 dB per doubling.
P4: Relates it to SDR: a wideband ADC followed by digital down-conversion and decimation to a narrow channel gains this processing gain, and oversampling also relaxes the analog anti-aliasing filter.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that plain oversampling (without noise shaping) gives 6 dB (a full bit) per doubling of the sample rate.
numeric_tolerance: The gain is exactly 10 log10(OSR) dB (3.01 dB per doubling); 6.02 N + 1.76 dB is the full-scale sine SNR of an ideal N-bit quantiser.
sources:
Kester, Analog Devices Tutorial MT-001, 'Taking the mystery out of the infamous formula SNR = 6.02N + 1.76dB, and why you should care' (2009) (process gain 10 log10(fs/(2 BW)))
Oppenheim and Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed., section 4.9 (oversampling and noise shaping in A/D conversion)

checker_1_note: note: P1 (white quantisation noise spread to fs/2, filtered to B, fraction 1/OSR remains), P2 (10 log10(OSR): 3 dB per doubling, half a bit), P3 (needs white, uncorrelated noise; noise shaping gives more) and P4 (DDC and decimation in SDR; relaxed anti-alias filter) are right. My 8-bit simulation with a little input noise shows the in-band quantisation noise falling 6.0 dB per factor 4 (52.4, 46.4, 40.4 dB at OSR 1, 4, 16). D1 (6 dB per doubling without noise shaping) is a real error; the tolerance text is exact.
checker_2_source: Kester, Analog Devices MT-001 (2009): SNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB + 10 log10(fs/(2 BW)); Oppenheim and Schafer, 3rd ed., sec. 4.9 (oversampled A/D conversion, noise shaping). Own simulation: 8-bit quantiser, in-band SNR at OSR 1, 4, 16, 64.

question: How can DSP be used to implement a software-defined equalizer to compensate for multipath fading in a communication channel?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States the problem and the aim: multipath makes the channel act as a filter (delayed, scaled copies; frequency-selective fading) that causes intersymbol interference, and an equaliser is a digital filter that approximately inverts the channel so that the combined response is close to an impulse (flat).
P2 (w=2): Names the structures and criteria: a linear FIR (transversal) equaliser, with zero-forcing (channel inversion, which amplifies noise where the channel response is small) or MMSE design; a decision-feedback equaliser that cancels the ISI of past symbols; or MLSE (Viterbi) detection.
P3 (w=2): States how the taps are found and kept up to date: adaptive algorithms such as LMS (or NLMS, RLS) trained on a known sequence or preamble, then decision-directed or blind (CMA) operation to track a time-varying channel, with the step size trading convergence speed against residual error.

question: Explain the role of DSP in implementing a software-defined beamformer for a phased array antenna system.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States the core role: the signal of each element (or subarray) is digitised and DSP applies a complex weight (phase shift and amplitude) to each channel and sums them, y = w^H x, so the beam is formed and steered in software by the phase progression across the array (for a ULA, exp(-j 2 pi n d sin(theta) / lambda)), with no moving parts.
P2: States that DSP calibrates the array: it estimates and removes the phase, gain and timing differences between the receive channels, which coherent combining requires.
P3 (w=2): Names at least two further functions DSP enables, for example amplitude tapering for sidelobe control; adaptive beamforming (for example MVDR or LMS) that places nulls on interferers using the estimated covariance; several simultaneous beams from the same samples; direction-of-arrival estimation (scanning, MUSIC); true time delay (fractional-delay filters) for wideband signals, where phase-only steering squints.
P4: States the implementation demands: synchronised sampling of all channels (common reference and LO) and a computational load that grows with the number of channels and the sample rate (often FPGA or GPU).

question: Explain the difference between stream tags and message passing in GNU Radio. When would you use each?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Describes stream tags: key:value metadata (PMTs) attached to one specific item (an absolute sample offset) of a data stream, which travel downstream with the samples through the blocks' work functions and are carried across rate changes by the tag propagation policy.
P2 (w=2): Describes message passing: asynchronous PMT messages sent between message ports (registered output and input ports, published with message_port_pub and handled by a message handler), not tied to any sample, and able to go upstream or to blocks that have no stream ports.
P3 (w=2): States when to use each: tags when information must line up with particular samples (for example a burst or packet start and length, receive timestamps, a frequency change, a correlator's timing estimate); messages for control and events not tied to a sample (for example retuning or gain commands to a USRP, GUI events, packets as PDUs, links to other applications).
P4: States the costs: many tags add processing overhead, and messages give no timing guarantee relative to the data stream.
disqualifying_errors: D1: Swaps the two (says tags are asynchronous and not tied to samples, or that messages are aligned to sample offsets).

question: Explain the concept of Gray coding in QPSK. Why is it used, and how does it affect error performance?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that Gray coding labels the four QPSK points so that neighbouring points differ in only one bit (for example 00, 01, 11, 10 going round the circle at 45, 135, 225 and 315 degrees).
P2 (w=2): Explains why: at useful SNRs the most likely symbol error is to a neighbouring point, so with Gray coding a symbol error usually costs one bit, giving BER close to SER/2 (SER/log2 M in general), the lowest BER for that SER.
P3: States the effect on performance: Gray-coded QPSK has the same BER as BPSK at the same Eb/N0, Pb = Q(sqrt(2 Eb/N0)); a non-Gray (natural binary) labelling has the same SER but a higher BER, because some neighbour errors flip both bits.
P4: States that Gray coding changes only the bit labels, not the constellation points or the symbol error rate.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that Gray coding lowers the symbol error rate or changes the constellation geometry.
sources:
Proakis and Salehi, Digital Communications, 5th ed., ch. 4 (Gray mapping; bit error probability of Gray-coded QPSK equals BPSK)

question: What is the purpose of a finite impulse response (FIR) filter in DSP, and how does it differ from an IIR filter?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States what an FIR filter is and does: each output is a weighted sum of the current and past inputs only, y[n] = sum_(k=0..N-1) b_k x[n - k] (a convolution with a finite impulse response of N taps), used to shape the frequency content of a signal (low-pass, high-pass, band-pass; removing noise or interference, anti-aliasing before decimation, pulse shaping, matched filtering).
P2 (w=2): States how an IIR filter differs: it uses feedback of past outputs, y[n] = sum b_k x[n - k] - sum a_k y[n - k], so its impulse response is infinitely long (it has poles).
P3 (w=2): States the practical consequences: an FIR filter is always stable and can have exactly linear phase (symmetric taps), but needs more taps for a sharp response; an IIR filter reaches a sharp response with far fewer coefficients but has nonlinear phase and can be unstable or sensitive to coefficient quantisation.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that FIR filters use feedback or can be unstable, or that IIR filters have exactly linear phase.
sources:
Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing, ch. 14 'Introduction to Digital Filters' (FIR by convolution, IIR by recursion) and ch. 21 'Filter Comparison'
Oppenheim and Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed., ch. 5 and 7 (FIR and IIR systems, linear phase, stability)

question: Explain how the 'ZMQ PUB Sink' and 'ZMQ SUB Source' blocks enable communication between separate GNU Radio flowgraphs or processes.
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States how the pair works: the ZMQ PUB Sink sends the stream items (of a chosen type and vector length) out on a ZeroMQ socket at an endpoint address (for example tcp://127.0.0.1:5555), and a ZMQ SUB Source in another flowgraph or process, on the same or another machine, connects to that address and feeds the received items into its own flowgraph.
P2 (w=2): States the publish-subscribe behaviour: one publisher can feed several subscribers; by default (On Full Buffer: Drop) the publisher does not wait for them, and data is dropped when no subscriber is connected or a subscriber falls behind (high-water mark), so delivery of every sample is not guaranteed.
P3 (w=2): States what both ends must agree on: the data are raw items with no format, so the item type, vector length and sample rate must match, as must the Pass Tags and Filter Key settings that change the wire format; by default the stream sink binds and the source connects, and an endpoint may have only one bind.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that PUB/SUB, with its default settings, guarantees delivery of every sample (back-pressure from the subscriber to the publisher).

question: If stream tags are not appearing at the output of a flowgraph, what are the possible causes, and how would you debug this issue?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that a block's tag propagation policy can stop tags: the default is All-to-All, but a block set to TPP_DONT ('Dont') passes no tags on unless its work function re-creates them, and some blocks remove tags on purpose (for example a Tag Gate, or a Channel Model with 'Block Tag Propagation' set to Yes).
P2 (w=2): States that tags must be attached at absolute item offsets (nitems_written(0) + i inside work); a block that uses the relative index i, or a rate-changing general block whose relative rate is unset or wrong, puts tags on the wrong items or loses them.
P3: States that the tag may never be produced or may be filtered out: the upstream block does not emit it, emits it under another key than the one looked for, or a key filter downstream (for example Tag Debug's 'Key Filter') does not match it.

question: Explain the difference between decimation and interpolation. When would you use each in a GNU Radio flowgraph?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that decimation by an integer M lowers the sample rate to fs/M (keeping one sample in M) and so lowers the representable bandwidth to fs/(2M); a low-pass (anti-aliasing) filter with cutoff below fs/(2M) must come before the sample dropping, otherwise out-of-band components alias.
P2 (w=2): States that interpolation by an integer L raises the sample rate to L*fs (inserting L-1 zeros, or repeating samples, between input samples) followed by a low-pass (anti-imaging) filter that removes the spectral images; it adds no new signal content.
P3: Gives when to use decimation, for example after tuning or channel selection to bring a wide SDR stream down to the rate the signal needs (less computation), or to match a slower sink such as a 48 kHz audio sink.
P4: Gives when to use interpolation, for example to raise a stream to the rate a sink or transmitter needs (an audio sink or SDR sink), or to create several samples per symbol for pulse shaping.
P5: Names GNU Radio blocks for each: a Decimating FIR Filter (or a Low Pass Filter or Frequency Xlating FIR Filter with a Decimation parameter) for decimation, an Interpolating FIR Filter for interpolation, and a Rational Resampler (interpolation L, decimation M) for a ratio L/M.
disqualifying_errors: D1: Swaps the two, stating that decimation raises the sample rate or that interpolation lowers it.

question: Why is an anti-aliasing filter necessary before decimation? What happens if it is omitted?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States why the filter is needed: after decimation by M the new rate fs/M can only represent frequencies up to fs/(2M), so the filter must remove everything above that new Nyquist frequency before samples are dropped.
P2 (w=2): States what happens without it: components above fs/(2M) (other signals, interferers and noise) alias, folding into the band 0 to fs/(2M) at frequencies offset by multiples of fs/M (for example a 130 kHz tone at fs = 1 MHz decimated by 10 appears at 30 kHz), corrupting the wanted signal and raising the noise floor.
P3: States that the aliasing cannot be removed afterwards, because the folded components overlap the wanted band and are indistinguishable from it.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that omitting the filter only loses the out-of-band components (they simply disappear) or only reduces resolution or amplitude, without saying that they fold into the band.

question: What is the relationship between SNR and bit error rate (BER) in a digital communication system? How would you plot this in GNU Radio?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that BER falls monotonically as SNR (or Eb/N0) rises, steeply for uncoded modulation in AWGN (the 'waterfall' curve, roughly exponential at high SNR), and that it is plotted as BER on a logarithmic axis against Eb/N0 or SNR in dB.
P2: Gives an AWGN formula for at least one modulation, for example BPSK (and Gray-coded QPSK) BER = Q(sqrt(2Eb/N0)) = 0.5 erfc(sqrt(Eb/N0)), about 1e-5 near 9.6 dB.
P3: Relates SNR to Eb/N0 (Eb/N0 = SNR * B/Rb, or Es/N0 = log2(M) * Eb/N0) and states that the curve depends on the modulation order, coding and channel (higher-order modulation needs more Eb/N0 for the same BER).
P4 (w=2): Describes a GNU Radio simulation that measures BER: a random bit source, a modulator, noise added at a known level (Noise Source plus Add, or a Channel Model's Noise Voltage set from the target SNR), a demodulator or decision block, and a comparison with the transmitted bits delayed to match the receiver latency (Delay block), using the BER block (fec ber_bf, which takes packed bytes and outputs log10 of the BER) or an XOR-and-count.
P5: States how the curve is obtained: repeat the measurement over a range of noise levels (a script loop, a QT GUI Range variable on the noise amplitude, or BER Curve Gen. with the QT GUI Bercurve Sink), counting enough errors per point, and plot BER on a log scale against Eb/N0 or SNR in dB.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that BER increases as SNR increases.

question: Design a GNU Radio flowgraph that injects AWGN noise into a signal and measures the resulting BER. What blocks would you use?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Gives a data source and modulator: random bits or bytes (Random Source, or a Vector Source with random data) mapped to symbols, for example with a Constellation Modulator or Chunks to Symbols (BPSK symbol table [-1, 1]).
P2 (w=2): Gives the noise injection: a Noise Source (Gaussian) added to the signal with an Add block, or a Channel Model with its Noise Voltage parameter, with the noise amplitude set from the target SNR or Eb/N0 (the Noise Source amplitude is the noise RMS, so amplitude = sqrt(signal power / 10^(SNR_dB/10))).
P3 (w=2): Gives the receiver decision: a demodulator or slicer that turns the noisy symbols back into bits, for example a Constellation Decoder or a Binary Slicer (with matched filtering and synchronisation in a full receiver chain).
P4 (w=2): Gives the BER measurement: the transmitted bits, delayed to line up with the received bits (Delay block) when the receiver has latency and in the same packing (Pack K Bits or Unpack K Bits as needed), compared with the received bits by the BER block (fec ber_bf, packed bytes in, log10 of the BER out) or by XOR and averaging, shown on a QT GUI Number Sink or stored in a sink.

question: What is a baseband signal, and how does it differ from a passband signal?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that a baseband signal has its spectrum around 0 Hz (from DC or near DC up to its bandwidth), not moved onto a carrier, for example audio, video or an NRZ line code.
P2 (w=2): States that a passband signal has its spectrum centred on a carrier frequency fc well away from 0 Hz (occupying a band around fc), produced by modulating or up-converting a baseband signal onto the carrier, and is the form sent over a radio channel.
P3: States how they relate: mixing with the carrier converts between them (up-conversion and down-conversion), and a band-limited passband signal is represented without loss by its complex baseband equivalent (I/Q, the complex envelope) of the same bandwidth, which is what SDRs and GNU Radio process, at a sample rate set by the bandwidth rather than by fc.
disqualifying_errors: D1: Swaps the two, stating that a baseband signal is centred on the carrier frequency or that a passband signal is centred at 0 Hz.

question: What is the purpose of sampling in digital signal processing, and how does it enable the conversion of analog signals to digital?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that sampling turns a continuous-time signal into a discrete-time sequence of values x[n] = x(n*Ts) taken at regular intervals Ts = 1/fs, which a computer can store and process as numbers.
P2 (w=2): States the sampling theorem: a signal band-limited to B Hz is completely determined by, and can be reconstructed from, its samples when fs > 2B (the Nyquist rate); sampling more slowly causes aliasing, where frequencies above fs/2 appear as lower frequencies.
P3: States that analog-to-digital conversion also quantises each sample's amplitude to a finite number of bits (a binary code), which adds quantisation error (about 6 dB of signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio per bit), so sampling discretises time and quantisation discretises amplitude.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that a sampling rate equal to the signal's highest frequency (rather than more than twice it) is enough to represent a real signal.

question: Explain the difference between ideal sampling and practical sampling (e.g., using an ADC). What are the limitations of practical sampling?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Describes ideal sampling: multiplication by a train of Dirac impulses, giving instantaneous samples at exact instants n*Ts with unlimited amplitude precision; the spectrum is the input spectrum repeated every fs, so a signal band-limited to B and sampled at fs > 2B is recovered exactly by an ideal low-pass (sinc) reconstruction filter.
P2 (w=2): Describes practical sampling in an ADC: a sample-and-hold takes each sample over a finite aperture or holds it for a time (flat-top samples), and the held value is quantised to a finite number of bits; reconstruction uses a zero-order-hold DAC and a non-ideal filter.
P3: Names quantisation as a limitation: a finite number of bits adds quantisation error, giving a signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio of about 6.02N + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine (74 dB for 12 bits), and the input range is limited (clipping).
P4: Names the anti-aliasing limitation: real filters have a finite transition band, so the signal is never strictly band-limited; practical systems sample faster than 2B (oversampling, a guard band) and some aliasing remains.
P5: Names at least two further limitations, for example sampling-clock jitter or aperture uncertainty (SNR limit -20*log10(2*pi*f*sigma_t), 64 dB at 100 MHz with 1 ps rms), the sinc droop of the hold (about -3.9 dB at fs/2 for a zero-order hold), limited analog input bandwidth, non-linearity (INL/DNL, spurs), thermal noise, or a maximum sample rate.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that practical sampling above 2B reproduces the analog signal exactly, with no quantisation error or other loss.
sources:
Oppenheim and Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed., sections 4.1-4.3 (periodic sampling with an impulse train, its frequency-domain representation, ideal reconstruction) and 4.8 (prefiltering to avoid aliasing, A/D conversion as sample-and-hold plus quantiser, analysis of quantisation errors, D/A conversion with a zero-order hold)
Derivation of the jitter limit: for x(t) = A sin(2 pi f t), a timing error dt gives an error of about 2 pi f A cos(2 pi f t) dt; with rms jitter sigma_t the error power is (2 pi f A sigma_t)^2 / 2 against the signal power A^2 / 2, so SNR = -20 log10(2 pi f sigma_t)

question: If a GNU Radio flowgraph is producing aliased output, how would you diagnose and fix the issue?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Gives a way to confirm aliasing: look at the spectrum (QT GUI Frequency Sink or Waterfall Sink) before and after each rate-changing block, or feed a test tone and sweep its frequency; aliased components appear at wrong frequencies, folded about half the sample rate of the stage, and move the wrong way or wrap around as the input frequency changes. The first stage where they appear locates the problem.
P2 (w=2): Names the usual causes: a decimation with no or too weak low-pass filtering (Keep 1 in N, or filter taps whose cutoff or transition band reaches above the new fs/2), a resampler with unsuitable taps, or a source whose sample rate is too low for its content (for example a Signal Source frequency above samp_rate/2, or an SDR whose analog bandwidth passes more than the sample rate).
P3: States that every block's sample-rate parameter must equal the actual rate of its input stream after earlier decimation or interpolation; filter taps designed for the wrong rate put the cutoff in the wrong place.
P4 (w=2): Gives the fix: put a low-pass filter with cutoff below the output Nyquist frequency (output rate / 2) and enough stopband attenuation before every decimation, for example a Decimating FIR Filter, a Low Pass Filter with its Decimation parameter, or a Rational Resampler with proper taps, instead of dropping samples; or raise the sample rate (and set the SDR's analog bandwidth) so that the signal fits below fs/2.
disqualifying_errors: D1: Proposes a Throttle block as the fix for aliasing (Throttle only paces the processing and does not change the samples).

question: What is the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), and how does it differ from the continuous Fourier Transform?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): Defines the DFT of N samples: X[k] = sum over n = 0..N-1 of x[n] e^(-j 2 pi k n / N), for k = 0..N-1 (inverse x[n] = (1/N) sum of X[k] e^(j 2 pi k n / N)), mapping N time samples to N complex frequency coefficients.
P2 (w=2): States the difference: the continuous Fourier transform X(f) = integral of x(t) e^(-j 2 pi f t) dt takes a continuous-time signal (possibly of infinite duration) to a continuous function of frequency, while the DFT takes a finite number of discrete samples to a finite number of discrete frequencies, so it can be computed.
P3: States that the DFT values are samples of the spectrum of the sampled sequence (the DTFT, periodic in fs) at the N frequencies f_k = k*fs/N, so the bin spacing (resolution) is fs/N.
P4: States a consequence of finite, discrete data: the DFT treats the N samples as one period of a periodic signal (x[n] and X[k] are N-periodic), which causes spectral leakage for tones that do not complete a whole number of cycles (reduced by windowing), and sampling in time makes the spectrum periodic (aliasing if undersampled).
sources:

PySDR, chapter 'Frequency Domain' (Fourier transform, FFT, FFT size and frequency bins)

question: Design a GNU Radio flowgraph that computes the DFT of a finite-length signal. What blocks would you use?

question: What is Power Spectral Density (PSD), and how does it describe the distribution of power in a signal over frequency?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that the PSD gives a signal's power per unit bandwidth as a function of frequency (units such as W/Hz or dBm/Hz).
P2 (w=2): States that integrating the PSD over a frequency band gives the power in that band, and integrating over all frequencies gives the total (average) power of the signal.
P3: States that, for a wide-sense stationary random signal, the PSD is the Fourier transform of the signal's autocorrelation function (Wiener-Khinchin theorem).
disqualifying_errors: D1: Describes the PSD as the amplitude or phase spectrum (volts, or the FFT values themselves) rather than power per unit frequency.

question: How does the Fourier Transform of a rectangular pulse look in the frequency domain?
required_points:
P1 (w=3): States that the Fourier transform of a rectangular pulse is a sinc function: for amplitude A and duration T, |X(f)| = A T |sinc(f T)| = |A sin(pi f T) / (pi f)|, peaking at A T at f = 0.
P2: States that the spectrum has nulls at the non-zero integer multiples of 1/T, so the main lobe is 2/T wide (null to null).
P3: States the inverse relation between pulse duration and spectral width: a shorter pulse gives a wider spectrum, and a longer pulse a narrower one.
P4: States that the side lobes decay slowly (as 1/f), the first one about 13 dB below the main-lobe peak, so the spectrum is not band-limited.
disqualifying_errors: D1: Claims the spectrum of a rectangular pulse is itself rectangular or band-limited (confusing it with the sinc-pulse / rectangular-spectrum dual).
sources:
Oppenheim and Willsky, Signals and Systems, chapter 4, the continuous-time Fourier transform of a rectangular pulse (a sinc function) and the time-frequency duality
PySDR, 'Frequency Domain' chapter (a rectangular pulse in time is a sinc in frequency; shorter in time means wider in frequency)
Code run: python sinc.py (numpy) for the first side-lobe level and the nulls
checker_1_source: Oppenheim and Willsky, Signals and Systems, 2nd ed., ch. 4 (the Fourier transform of a rectangular pulse is a sinc; time-frequency scaling); my own numpy computation of the first side lobe of sinc (below).
checker_1_note: note: P1 (sinc, |X(f)| = A T |sinc(f T)|, peak A T at f = 0), P2 (nulls at non-zero multiples of 1/T, main lobe 2/T), P3 (shorter pulse, wider spectrum) and P4 (side lobes fall as 1/f, first one about 13 dB down, not band-limited) are right. The first side lobe of |sinc| is at f T = 1.430, 13.26 dB below the peak. D1 (rectangular or band-limited spectrum) is the confusion the question tests.
checker_2_source: Oppenheim and Willsky, Signals and Systems, 2nd ed., sec. 4.2 (Fourier transform of a rectangular pulse: 2 sin(omega T1)/omega, a sinc) and sec. 4.3.6 (duality). Own check: |sinc(fT)| has nulls at k/T and a first side lobe of -13.26 dB; a numerical FT of a unit pulse of duration 1 gives 1.000 at f = 0 and 0.637 at f = 0.5/T.
checker_2_note: note: All points are correct and decidable; P1 carries the answer with weight 3. My run confirms P2 and P4 (nulls at multiples of 1/T, first side lobe -13.26 dB, 1/f decay). D1 is the duality confusion the question tests.

question: What is a spectrogram, and how is it generated from a signal?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that a spectrogram is a time-frequency picture of a signal: one axis is time, the other frequency, and the colour or intensity shows the power (squared magnitude, often in dB) at each time and frequency.
P2 (w=2): States that it is generated with the short-time Fourier transform: the signal is cut into short, often overlapping segments, each segment is windowed and transformed with an FFT, and the squared magnitudes of successive FFTs are stacked over time.
P3: States that the segment (FFT) length trades time resolution against frequency resolution: longer segments give finer frequency resolution and coarser time resolution.
disqualifying_errors: D1: Claims a spectrogram is a single FFT of the whole signal, with no time axis.
sources:
PySDR, 'Frequency Domain' chapter (spectrogram / waterfall: FFTs of successive blocks of samples stacked over time)
Oppenheim and Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, chapter 10 (the time-dependent Fourier transform and the spectrogram; window length and resolution)

question: If an FIR filter introduces excessive delay, how can this be mitigated?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that a linear-phase FIR filter with N taps delays every frequency by the same (N-1)/2 samples, so the delay grows with the number of taps, which a narrow transition band (relative to the sample rate) forces up.
P2 (w=2): Reduces the number of taps: relaxes the transition width or ripple specification, or uses an optimal (equiripple, Parks-McClellan) design that meets the same specification with fewer taps.
P3: Names at least one further mitigation, for example a minimum-phase FIR or an IIR filter that gives a similar magnitude response with much less delay at the cost of non-linear phase; compensating the known constant delay where only alignment matters (delaying the other paths by (N - 1)/2 samples); or filtering in stages at a lower sample rate (multistage or polyphase decimation) so that fewer taps are needed.
disqualifying_errors: D1: Claims that a linear-phase FIR's delay depends on frequency (distorting the signal) rather than being a constant (N-1)/2 samples.
sources:
Oppenheim and Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, chapter 5 (generalized linear phase: a symmetric FIR of length N has a constant group delay of (N-1)/2 samples; minimum-phase systems) and chapter 7 (FIR design by windowing and the Parks-McClellan algorithm)

question: If an IIR filter exhibits instability, what could be the cause, and how would you fix it?
required_points:
P1 (w=2): States that an IIR filter is unstable when one or more poles of its transfer function lie on or outside the unit circle, and that checking the pole magnitudes (all must be below 1) diagnoses it.
P2 (w=2): Names finite-precision coefficient quantization in a high-order direct-form realization as a common cause: poles close to the unit circle (narrow bandwidth or a cutoff that is small relative to the sample rate) move outside it when the coefficients are rounded.
P3 (w=2): Fixes it by realizing the filter as a cascade of second-order sections (biquads), using higher-precision (double) coefficients and arithmetic, or lowering the order or redesigning so the poles sit safely inside the unit circle.
P4 (w=0.5): Names another cause or fix, for example a design or implementation error such as a wrong sign convention for the feedback coefficients (GNU Radio's IIR Filter 'Old Style of Taps'), or replacing the filter by an FIR filter, which has no feedback and is always stable.
disqualifying_errors: D1: States that the filter is stable when its poles are outside the unit circle, or puts the stability condition on the zeros instead of the poles.
sources:
Oppenheim and Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, chapter 6 (structures for discrete-time systems: effects of coefficient quantization on pole locations, cascade of second-order sections) and chapter 3 (a causal system is stable when all poles lie inside the unit circle)

A 10th-order Butterworth low-pass (cutoff 0.02) has largest pole magnitude 0.9892 in double precision, 1.3072 with float32 direct-form coefficients and 0.9902 as float32 second-order sections.
